messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 26
- Gender: Female
- Ethnicity: Latin American
- Relationship Status: Single
- Occupation: Student
- Trauma Type: Toxic chemical exposure
- Pcl5: 70

She is twenty-six, a graduate student in environmental chemistry, and she tells me this story in fragments, as if each piece carries its own weight of danger. She sits on the edge of the chair, hands folded in her lap, eyes scanning the room once before settling on the floor. The trauma happened two years ago, during her second year of a master’s program, in a lab she now refuses to name.

It was late evening, near the end of a long synthesis procedure. She was alone, running a reaction with a volatile solvent—dichloromethane, she says, though she whispers the word now as if it might escape the bottle again. A seal failed. A spray of liquid hit her face, her arms, her chest. The sharp, sweet smell filled her nostrils. She fumbled for the emergency shower, but by the time she reached it, her skin was already burning. She rinsed for ten minutes, then went to the campus health center. They told her it was minor, gave her a topical cream, sent her home.

But the smell stayed. In the days that followed, she washed her hair three times a day, scrubbed her arms raw, but the chemical scent clung to her memory. She started having nightmares: her lab coat melting into her skin, her lungs filling with liquid glass, the fume hood a silent, gaping mouth. She stopped going to lab. She told her advisor she had family issues. She took an Incomplete in her advanced synthesis course.

Now, two years later, she is still a student—technically. She has switched to a theoretical track that requires no bench work. Her thesis involves computational modeling of reaction pathways. She works from home, in a studio apartment where she has removed all cleaning products and stores her shampoo in a sealed bin. She cannot walk past a janitor’s closet without her breath catching. Once, on the bus, a passenger opened a bottle of nail polish remover, and she vomited into her own hands.

She avoids certain streets. She avoids campus after dark. She avoids the wing of the chemistry building entirely. If a classmate mentions a lab accident in any context, she excuses herself to the restroom and stares at her reflection until her heart slows. She has lost friends—they don’t understand why she can’t just “get over it,” why she flinches at perfume, why she wears long sleeves even in summer. She tells me she has become a ghost in her own life, moving through hallways with her head down, never looking at glassware.

The PCL-5 score of 70 confirms what I already sense: the intrusion, the avoidance, the hyperarousal are relentless. She describes a constant, low-level vigilance, as if the world itself is a leaky container. She checks seals on water bottles. She holds her breath when passing garbage trucks. She cannot taste foods that remind her of the lab’s chemical odor—artificial fruit flavors, mint, glue. Her sleep is fractured. She wakes gasping, convinced she can smell that sweet, burning vapor again.

But she does not connect these experiences to the event. She tells me she is just being careful. She tells me she is fine, as long as she controls her environment. She has not been to a lab in eighteen months. She has not spoken to her former lab mates. She has not told her parents what happened—they are in another country, and she does not want them to worry. So she carries the story alone, under layers of avoidance and self-blame, convinced that if she had only checked the seal, if she had only been faster, she would not be sitting here, describing her life as a series of landmines.
